# Validation rules, inferred schemas and synthetic stand-ins

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rmoriebricklayer)
```

A capsule says what shape its data must have. This vignette covers the three tools for
stating and checking that shape: explicit **rules**, a **schema** inferred from a known-good
table, and a **synthetic stand-in** generated from the schema when the portal is unreachable.

## Rules

A rule is a name, a predicate and optionally a column. Row-wise rules report how many rows
fail and which; table-wise rules take the whole data frame. A `fatal` severity stops the
pipeline; a `warning` is recorded.

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-rules}
df <- data.frame(id = c(1, 2, 2), age = c(30, -5, 40),
                 start = c(1, 5, 3), end = c(2, 4, 9))

rules <- list(
  rul("agenonnegative", function(v) v >= 0, col = "age"),
  rul("idunique", function(v) !anyDuplicated(v), col = "id", sev = "fatal"),
  rul("datesordered", function(d) all(d$start <= d$end))
)

issues <- valrules(df, rules)
names(issues)
issues$agenonnegative$n_failed
issues$agenonnegative$rows
```

Clean data produces nothing:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-rules-clean}
clean <- data.frame(id = 1:3, age = c(30, 31, 40), start = 1:3, end = 4:6)
length(valrules(clean, rules))
```

Two behaviours matter for trust. A rule for an absent column is **skipped**, not failed: a
missing column is the schema's finding to report. And a rule that *errors* is a **failure**,
never a silent pass:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-rules-edge}
length(valrules(data.frame(id = 1:3), rules[1:2]))
broken <- list(rul("bad", function(v) stop("boom"), col = "age"))
valrules(clean, broken)$bad$message
```

### Ready-made rules

Common checks have constructors so the intent is in the name:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-ready}
rules2 <- list(
  rulenull("id"),
  ruleuniq("id", sev = "fatal"),
  rulebtw("age", 0, 120),
  ruleinset("grade", c("a", "b", "c")),
  rulerx("code", "^[A-Z]{2}-[0-9]{4}$"),
  rulemad("score", n = 3),
  rulecolcnt(6, sev = "fatal")
)
length(rules2)
```

`ruleincr()`, `ruledstn()` and `rulecmpl()` complete the set.
`schval(df, rules2)` runs a rule list the same way and stops on any fatal
issue, which is the call a pipeline makes (it takes a provenance list or a rule list; until
0.5.12 a rule list was silently ignored and reported a pass).

## Inferring a schema

Given a table known to be right, `infsch()` pins what can be pinned: column names and
types, numeric ranges with a little slack, and the level set of categorical columns (up to
`maxlvl`, so free text is not mistaken for a code list):

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-infer}
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(
  id = 1:100,
  score = stats::runif(100, 0, 10),
  grade = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 100, TRUE),
  note = paste0("free text ", 1:100),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sch <- infsch(df)
sch$expected_value_sets
```

It validates the table it was learned from, and catches a vanished column or a new
category:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-infer-check}
length(valsch(df, list(schema = sch)))
length(valsch(df[, -3], list(schema = sch))) > 0
bad <- df
bad$grade[1] <- "z"
length(valsch(bad, list(schema = sch))) > 0
```

A schema goes into the capsule's provenance record; `valsch()` is what
`vrfcps()` runs on a fresh download.

## Synthetic stand-ins

When the portal is down, the pipeline should still run end to end on data of the right
shape, clearly marked as synthetic. A recipe names each column's generator:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-synthetic}
recipe <- list(
  n_rows = 20, seed = 42,
  columns = list(
    year   = list(type = "sample", values = list(2024, 2025)),
    alert  = list(type = "bernoulli", p = 0.2),
    visits = list(type = "poisson", lambda = 3, min = 1),
    id     = list(type = "id_pattern", pattern = "p-{seq:05d}")
  )
)
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
res <- mksyncsv(recipe, out)
res$rows
res$seed

df <- utils::read.csv(out)
dim(df)
names(df)
head(df, 3)
```

The seed makes the stand-in reproducible; `nrows` overrides the recipe's own count. A
`<path>.synthetic` sidecar file is written beside the CSV (the file itself stays a plain
table), and the capsule checks read that marker, so a synthetic run can never be mistaken
for a result:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-synthetic-mark}
mksyncsv(recipe, tempfile(fileext = ".csv"), nrows = 5)$rows
```

`mksyncol()` generates one column from a spec, for building a table piece by
piece or for testing a generator.

## Putting them together

1. On the first, trusted download: `infsch()`, then add the rules the schema cannot
   express (ordering between columns, cross-table consistency) and pin both.
2. On every later run: `valsch()` and `valrules()`; stop on `fatal`.
3. When the source is unreachable: `mksyncsv()` from the pinned schema, run the
   pipeline, and let the synthetic marker say what the output is.


## Rules for a published table

Rules catch problems in a table before it is used. For an Indigenous health table: the
estimate inside its interval, a known quality flag, and a known group:

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-indigenous-rules}
d <- indiex("health")
rules <- list(
  ruleinset("quality", c("ok", "E", "F", "x", "..")),
  ruleinset("group", c("First Nations", "M\u00e9tis", "Inuit", "Non-Indigenous")),
  rul("estimate inside its interval",
       function(x) is.na(x$estimate) | (x$lower <= x$estimate & x$estimate <= x$upper))
)
valrules(d, rules)
```

An empty list means every rule held on every row.

## The synthetic stand-in in a picture

The stand-in written above, column by column as the recipe generated it: visits drawn from a
Poisson distribution with mean 3 and never below 1, and the share of rows with an alert in each
year (the recipe asks for 20%).

```{r validation-rules-and-synthetic-data-synthetic-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(table(df$visits), col = blpal()[1], xlab = "visits", ylab = "rows",
        main = "Synthetic visits")
al <- tapply(df$alert == "Yes", df$year, mean)
barplot(100 * al, col = blpal()[2], ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "year", ylab = "rows with an alert (%)",
        main = "Synthetic alert flag")
abline(h = 20, lty = 2)
par(op)
```
